questions.title: Why ETL needs a staging layer
questions.prompt: Why do most ETL pipelines load source data into a staging table first, instead of transforming it directly from the source system straight into the warehouse's fact and dimension tables?
questions.modelAnswer: A staging table is a temporary, usually untransformed (or only lightly typed) landing spot for data pulled straight out of a source system, before any real business transformation happens. The main reasons to stage rather than transform directly in-flight: it gets the extract away from the fragile, often slow source connection as quickly as possible, so a transformation bug or a long-running join doesn't hold a connection open against a live production system any longer than necessary; it gives you a stable, local copy to re-run transformations against repeatedly while developing and debugging, without hitting the source again every time; and it creates a natural checkpoint to validate row counts and basic data quality before anything touches the real fact/dimension tables, so bad data can be caught and rejected in staging instead of corrupting the warehouse. Transforming directly from source to warehouse in one pass couples the pipeline's correctness entirely to the source system's availability and performance for the whole duration of the load, and makes it much harder to isolate whether a problem came from extraction, transformation, or load.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain staging as getting the data to safety first, then worrying about shaping it. The moment I've pulled rows into a staging table, I'm no longer dependent on the source system staying fast and available while I work out the transformation logic -- I can re-run my joins and lookups against the local staging copy as many times as I need while debugging, instead of hitting a live production database on every attempt. Staging also gives me a clean checkpoint: I can check row counts and basic data quality right there, before anything touches the real fact or dimension tables, which means a bad batch gets caught in staging instead of corrupting the warehouse. Skipping straight from source to warehouse in one pass means if something goes wrong, I have no way to tell whether the problem was in extraction, transformation, or load -- staging is what lets me isolate which stage actually broke.
commonMistakes: Skipping staging to 'save a step,' then having no way to isolate whether a bad load came from extraction, transformation, or load
Treating the staging table as if it needs the same constraints/indexes as the real warehouse tables
Holding a connection open against the live source for the entire transformation instead of extracting quickly into staging first
Not validating row counts or data quality at the staging checkpoint before loading into fact/dimension tables
keyPoints: Staging is a temporary landing area for source data before any real transformation happens
Staging minimizes how long the fragile source connection stays open
Staging gives a stable local copy to re-run and debug transformations against
Staging creates a checkpoint to validate data quality before it reaches the real warehouse tables

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a staging table is and when it's populated
Correctly explains the source-connection/performance benefit
Correctly explains the debugging/data-quality-checkpoint benefit

questions.title: Why warehouses use surrogate keys
questions.prompt: What's a surrogate key, and why do dimension tables in a warehouse typically use a warehouse-generated surrogate key as their primary key instead of just reusing the source system's natural key (like a CustomerID from the OLTP database)?
questions.modelAnswer: A natural key is whatever already uniquely identifies a row in the source system -- a CustomerID, a ProductCode -- and it has business meaning outside the warehouse. A surrogate key is a meaningless, warehouse-generated identifier (almost always a simple incrementing integer) created purely to be the dimension table's own primary key, with no meaning to the business at all. Warehouses use surrogate keys instead of natural keys for a few concrete reasons: a surrogate key insulates the warehouse from the source system changing its own key format or reusing an old ID; it lets a single natural key have more than one row in the dimension at once, which is exactly what SCD Type 2 versioning requires -- the same CustomerID needs multiple surrogate-keyed rows over time as attributes change, something a natural key alone could never support as a primary key; and it keeps join performance predictable, since a simple integer join is typically faster and more compact than joining on a source system's natural key, which might be a longer string or a composite key. The natural key doesn't disappear -- it's still stored as a regular column on the dimension (often called the business key) for traceability back to the source, it's just no longer the column other tables join against.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd define it by contrast: the natural key is whatever ID the source system already uses -- CustomerID, say -- and it carries real business meaning. The surrogate key is just a meaningless integer I generate inside the warehouse, purely so the dimension has its own stable identity independent of the source. The concrete reason this matters is Type 2 history: if DimCustomer needs to keep two versions of the same customer around because an attribute changed, I can't use CustomerID as the primary key for both rows -- it would collide, since a primary key can't repeat. A surrogate key solves that cleanly, since each version just gets its own new integer. It also protects me if the source system ever changes its own ID scheme, or reuses an old ID for someone new, since my warehouse's own key never has to depend on the source staying consistent. I'd still keep CustomerID around as a normal column on the dimension -- just not as what other tables join against.
commonMistakes: Using the source system's natural key directly as the dimension's primary key, then being unable to support SCD Type 2 versioning
Thinking the natural key disappears entirely instead of still being stored as a regular (business key) column
Not realizing a surrogate key insulates the warehouse from the source system changing or reusing its own key values
Assuming surrogate keys are only about performance, missing the more fundamental Type 2 history requirement
keyPoints: Natural key: the source system's own identifier, with real business meaning
Surrogate key: a meaningless, warehouse-generated integer used as the dimension's primary key
Surrogate keys let the same natural key have multiple versioned rows (required for SCD Type 2)
The natural key is retained as a regular business-key column, just not used for joins

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines natural key vs. surrogate key
Correctly connects surrogate keys to SCD Type 2 versioning
Mentions insulation from source-system key changes and/or join performance

questions.title: What you'd say in your first stand-up
questions.prompt: What is a Daily Scrum (stand-up), and what would you actually say during one in your first week on a new BI team?
questions.modelAnswer: A Daily Scrum, commonly called a stand-up, is a short, time-boxed daily meeting -- often 15 minutes -- where the team synchronizes with itself on progress and blockers; it's explicitly not a status report delivered upward to a manager, it's the team talking to each other. The typical shape each person covers is roughly: what I did since the last stand-up, what I'm doing until the next one, and anything blocking me. A strong first-week answer from a junior team member stays specific and brief rather than vague: naming the actual ticket or task worked on, being honest and specific about being stuck rather than saying a vague 'I'm still working on it,' and flagging a blocker the moment it's identified rather than waiting to mention it, since the whole point of surfacing a blocker in stand-up is getting help from the team quickly, not saving face. A junior new hire should resist the urge to over-explain or justify slow progress at length -- stand-up is meant to be short, and a longer conversation about a specific blocker belongs in a follow-up afterward, not consuming the whole meeting.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep it short and specific, something like: 'Yesterday I finished writing the Lookup for the Customer dimension and started on the fact table load. Today I'm wiring up the error output so bad rows get redirected instead of failing the whole package. I'm blocked on getting read access to the QA staging database, so if anyone can help with that after stand-up, I'd appreciate it.' That covers all three parts -- what I did, what I'm doing, what's blocking me -- in under thirty seconds, and it names a real ticket instead of a vague status. I'd also remind myself that stand-up isn't the place to actually solve the blocker; it's the place to surface it so the right person can grab me right after.
commonMistakes: Treating stand-up like a status report to a manager instead of the team syncing with itself
Being vague ('still working on it') instead of naming the specific ticket or task
Saving a blocker until later instead of surfacing it the moment it's identified
Turning stand-up into a long problem-solving discussion instead of flagging it briefly and following up afterward
keyPoints: Daily Scrum/stand-up is short, time-boxed, and team-to-team, not a report to a manager
Typical shape: what I did, what I'm doing next, what's blocking me
Name specific work, not vague progress statements
Surface blockers immediately; save detailed discussion for after stand-up

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what a stand-up is and its purpose
Gives a specific, well-structured example of what to say
Avoids the common vague-status-report trap

questions.title: Recognizing 'blocked' vs. just behind
questions.prompt: You've been working on a ticket and progress has stalled. How do you tell whether you're just behind schedule or genuinely blocked, and how do you communicate that to your team?
questions.modelAnswer: 'Off Track' means the work is simply taking longer than planned -- normal, and usually just needs more time or a closer look, with progress still genuinely possible on your own. 'Blocked' means the work has hit a hard stop entirely outside your control -- a pending approval, a broken test environment, a dependency on another team -- where no amount of your own effort moves it forward until that's resolved. The practical test is asking: is there anything I can still personally do right now to make progress on this? If yes, it's Off Track -- keep working and simply mention in stand-up that it's taking longer than expected. If no -- you're waiting on someone or something outside your control -- it's Blocked, and it should be flagged clearly and immediately, not saved for the next scheduled meeting, since every day a real blocker goes unflagged is a day of work not getting unstuck sooner.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask myself one question: is there anything I can actually still do myself, right now, to move this forward? If the honest answer is yes -- I just need more time, or I need to think through the approach again -- that's Off Track, and I'd keep grinding and just flag in stand-up that it's taking longer than I estimated. If the honest answer is no -- I'm waiting on an approval, a broken environment, or someone on another team -- that's genuinely Blocked, and I wouldn't sit on it until the next stand-up. I'd flag it the moment I realize it, specifically naming what I actually need to get unblocked, rather than just saying 'I'm stuck,' because a specific ask is what actually gets someone to act on it quickly.
commonMistakes: Quietly grinding on a ticket without flagging it, assuming asking for help makes you look unprepared
Mislabeling 'off track' (just taking longer) as 'blocked' when there's still personal progress possible
Waiting until the next stand-up to mention a blocker instead of flagging it the moment it's identified
Flagging a blocker vaguely instead of saying specifically what's needed to unblock it
keyPoints: Off Track: work is simply taking longer than planned, more time/closer look resolves it
Blocked: a hard stop entirely outside your control -- no amount of personal effort moves it forward
The test: is there anything I can still do myself right now? If no, you're blocked
Flag a blocker immediately and specifically, not quietly or vaguely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes Off Track from Blocked
Gives a usable decision test for telling them apart
Describes a clear, prompt way to communicate a real blocker

questions.title: Explaining why the team works in sprints, not all at once
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why your team can't just build the whole report and show it to them when it's completely done, instead of working in two-week sprints. How would you explain the difference between Agile and Waterfall to them, and why your team works the way it does?
questions.modelAnswer: Waterfall fits work where the requirements are genuinely stable and fully understood up front, moving through fixed phases once in order -- but if a requirement turns out to be wrong, that's usually not discovered until most of the work is already built, which makes it expensive to fix at that point. Agile instead breaks the same work into short, repeating two-week cycles, each one producing something real and working that the stakeholder can actually see and react to. The explanation should connect directly to the stakeholder's own interest rather than staying abstract: working in sprints means they get to say 'that's not quite what I meant' after two weeks of effort instead of after two months, which protects them, not just the team. It's also worth clarifying that a sprint still produces a genuinely working, shippable piece of the report each cycle -- not an unfinished fragment -- so showing it early isn't showing something broken.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd skip straight to what's in it for them. If we built the whole thing in one long pass and only showed it at the end, and it turned out we misunderstood something on day one, we wouldn't find that out until the entire report was already built -- which is expensive and slow to fix at that point. Working in two-week sprints means every two weeks you get to look at something real and tell us if we're headed the wrong direction, while that's still cheap to correct. I'd also be clear that what you're seeing every two weeks isn't a half-finished mess -- it's a genuinely working slice of the report, just not the whole thing yet. That's really the whole point of sprints: catching a misunderstanding in week two instead of week eight.
commonMistakes: Explaining Agile/Waterfall in the abstract without connecting it to why it benefits this stakeholder specifically
Implying sprints mean nothing gets fully finished, instead of explaining a sprint still produces a real, shippable increment
Being dismissive of the stakeholder's preference instead of explaining the real trade-off
Using unexplained jargon (backlog, increment, retrospective) instead of plain language
keyPoints: Waterfall fits stable, well-understood requirements but surfaces mistakes late and expensively
Agile's short cycles let the stakeholder react to real progress every 1-2 weeks, catching misunderstandings early
Connect the explanation to the stakeholder's own interest, not an abstract process lecture
Each sprint still produces a real, working increment, not an unfinished fragment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately explains the Agile vs. Waterfall trade-off
Connects the explanation to the stakeholder's own interest
Communicates without unexplained jargon

questions.title: Responding to a pull request sent back for changes
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time a teammate reviewed your work -- a query, a package, or a report -- and sent it back with specific changes requested. How did you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a behavioral question testing professionalism and how a candidate handles feedback, not a request for a technical fact. A strong answer first frames code/report review correctly: it happens inside the Dev stage, before QA ever sees the change, as a normal second set of eyes on the approach -- not a personal judgment, and it's completely normal for a reviewer to send work back before it's allowed to merge. The answer should use the STAR structure (Situation, Task, Action, Result), with Action describing reading the specific feedback carefully, asking a clarifying question if the reasoning wasn't obvious rather than assuming or arguing, making the requested change (or explaining a respectful disagreement if there was a good reason), and re-requesting review. Result should state the concrete outcome -- the change was approved and merged, and ideally what was learned or changed going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell one specific story rather than describe my attitude toward feedback in general. Situation: on my capstone's SSIS package, a reviewer flagged that my Lookup transformation had no error output configured, so a non-matching row would silently fail the whole package instead of being handled. Task: I needed to understand why that mattered and fix it properly, not just make the comment go away. Action: I asked the reviewer to walk me through what would actually happen with a non-matching row, since I hadn't considered it, then I configured the error output to redirect those rows to a dedicated log table instead of failing the package, and re-requested review with a short note explaining what I'd changed and why. Result: it was approved on the second pass, and I started checking every Lookup's error output by default on everything I built after that, which is the kind of habit a good review catches before it becomes a real production incident.
commonMistakes: Taking review feedback personally instead of treating it as a normal part of the Dev stage
Making the requested change without understanding why it was requested
Arguing defensively instead of asking a clarifying question when the reasoning isn't clear
Describing review feedback in general terms instead of telling one specific, real story with a stated Result
keyPoints: Code/report review happens inside the Dev stage, before QA -- it's a normal second set of eyes, not a personal judgment
Read specific feedback carefully; ask a clarifying question if the reasoning isn't obvious
Make the change (or explain a respectful disagreement), then re-request review
Use STAR and state the concrete Result -- what happened after the change was made

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Frames review feedback as a normal part of the process, not a personal setback
Tells a specific, real story using STAR
States a concrete Result

questions.title: Communicating during a live production incident
questions.prompt: Two days after a dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it's showing zero sales for their region all month. Walk me through how you'd investigate, and what you would communicate to the manager while you're still figuring out the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the two parts of this question clearly. On investigation: start with the simplest explanation before anything complex -- did the dashboard's scheduled refresh actually run last night at all -- then work backward from the visible symptom toward the source, checking whether the ETL load completed for that region, whether the issue is in the underlying data or just a report-level filter, rather than guessing at a cause. On communication: send an honest, specific acknowledgment quickly -- confirming the report was received, that it's being looked into, and giving a concrete time to expect an update -- rather than staying silent until a fix is confirmed. It's expected and professional to communicate while still investigating, not only once the cause is found; silence during that window reads as neglect even when real work is happening behind the scenes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this into what I say and what I actually do, and do the communication part first. Within a few minutes I'd send something like: 'Thanks for flagging this -- I'm looking into it now and will have an update for you by end of day.' That costs me almost nothing and tells the manager they haven't been forgotten. Then I'd investigate from the simplest explanation outward: did last night's scheduled refresh actually complete, or did it fail silently? If the refresh ran fine, I'd check whether that region's rows actually loaded into the fact table for this month, or whether this is a filter or slicer issue purely inside the report itself. I'd keep narrowing from the visible symptom back toward the source rather than guessing at something exotic first. Once I actually find the cause, I'd follow up with a clear explanation of what happened and what I changed -- not just a silent fix with no note at all.
commonMistakes: Staying silent until the fix is confirmed instead of acknowledging the report and giving a timeframe while still investigating
Jumping straight to a complex theory instead of checking the simplest thing first (did the scheduled refresh even run)
Investigating only inside the report itself without checking whether the issue actually originates further upstream in the data pipeline
Not giving the manager a concrete time to expect an update, leaving them to wonder if it's been forgotten
keyPoints: Communicate an acknowledgment and a timeframe immediately, don't wait for the fix to say anything
Investigate by narrowing from the visible symptom back toward the source (refresh status, pipeline, source data)
Check the simplest explanation first (did the scheduled load actually run) before assuming something complex
Follow up with a clear explanation once the cause is found, not just a silent fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a logical investigation approach, working from symptom back to source
Correctly emphasizes communicating early, before the cause is known
Clarity and professionalism of the communication described

questions.title: Turning a vague business request into a user story
questions.prompt: A sales director emails you: 'Our regional managers keep asking me for last month's numbers by email. I need a dashboard that shows revenue by region and by product category, updated automatically, so they can check it themselves.' How would you turn that into a proper user story with acceptance criteria before you start building anything?
questions.modelAnswer: A user story is written from the user's point of view, in the shape 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' -- for this request: 'As a regional manager, I want a dashboard showing revenue by region and product category, so that I can check my own numbers without emailing the sales director.' A story alone is too vague to know when it's actually done, which is what acceptance criteria are for -- specific, checkable conditions, such as 'the dashboard reflects the prior day's closed sales by 7 AM each morning, with no manual steps' and 'the region filter defaults to the viewer's assigned territory.' Just as important is noticing what the original email left out: it never says what should happen when a region has zero sales for the month. A strong answer explicitly surfaces that gap -- either asking the sales director directly, or documenting a reasonable judgment call as its own acceptance criterion -- rather than silently guessing and discovering the wrong assumption after the dashboard is already built.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building from that email directly -- I'd turn it into a story first: 'As a regional manager, I want a dashboard showing revenue by region and product category, so that I can check my own numbers without emailing the sales director.' Then I'd write acceptance criteria that are actually checkable, not just a vague sense of done -- something like 'reflects yesterday's closed sales by 7 AM with no manual steps' and 'the region filter defaults to the viewer's own territory.' The thing I'd specifically flag before writing a single line of DAX is that the email never says what should happen if a region had zero sales that month -- show it as zero, blank, or leave it off the list entirely? I'd either ask the sales director directly or write down my own reasonable assumption as an explicit acceptance criterion, because guessing silently on that detail is exactly the kind of thing that comes back wrong during UAT.
commonMistakes: Starting to build directly from the vague email instead of writing a structured user story first
Writing a user story with no acceptance criteria, leaving 'done' undefined
Silently guessing at an ambiguous detail (like the zero-sales case) instead of asking or explicitly documenting the judgment call
Writing acceptance criteria that aren't actually checkable ('looks good') instead of specific and testable
keyPoints: User story shape: As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
Acceptance criteria must be specific and checkable, not vague
Explicitly surface and resolve ambiguous details (like the zero-sales edge case) before building
A story isn't ready to build until its acceptance criteria are defined

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correctly-shaped user story
Writes specific, checkable acceptance criteria
Identifies and resolves an ambiguous detail from the original request

questions.title: UNION vs. UNION ALL
questions.prompt: In T-SQL, what's the difference between UNION and UNION ALL when combining the result sets of two SELECT statements, and what two conditions must both SELECT statements satisfy before you can combine them at all?
questions.modelAnswer: UNION combines the rows returned by two (or more) SELECT statements into one result set and removes any duplicate rows from that combined set, which requires SQL Server to do an implicit sort/distinct pass over the whole combined output. UNION ALL also combines the rows, but keeps every row exactly as returned, duplicates included, and skips the dedup pass entirely -- which makes it faster and cheaper to run whenever duplicates either can't occur or genuinely don't matter. Both statements being combined must return the same number of columns, and the data type in each corresponding column position must be compatible (not necessarily identical, but implicitly convertible) -- column names in the final result come from the first SELECT statement, regardless of what the second one used.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd default to UNION ALL unless I actually have a reason to expect duplicates and need them removed, because UNION ALL skips the sort/distinct work UNION does under the hood, so it's just cheaper to run on anything beyond a trivial row count. The two things I always check before combining two SELECTs this way: same number of columns on both sides, and compatible data types lining up column-by-column -- if the second SELECT's third column is a different, incompatible type from the first's third column, the combine fails outright. One detail that trips people up is that the final column names come entirely from the first SELECT -- aliasing a column differently in the second query doesn't change anything in the output.
questions.example:
-- UNION: removes duplicate rows across both queries
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Person.Person WHERE LastName = 'Smith'
UNION
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM HumanResources.Employee e
JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = e.BusinessEntityID WHERE LastName = 'Smith';

-- UNION ALL: keeps every row, including duplicates, and skips the dedup work
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Person.Person WHERE LastName = 'Smith'
UNION ALL
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM HumanResources.Employee e
JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = e.BusinessEntityID WHERE LastName = 'Smith';
commonMistakes: Using UNION by default everywhere, paying for a dedup pass that isn't actually needed
Assuming the two SELECTs need identical column names instead of just a matching column count and compatible types
Not realizing the final result's column names come from the first SELECT, regardless of aliases used in the second
Forgetting ORDER BY can only appear once, at the very end of the combined statement, not after each individual SELECT
keyPoints: UNION removes duplicate rows across the combined result sets; UNION ALL keeps every row
UNION ALL is cheaper -- it skips the sort/distinct pass UNION performs
Both SELECTs must return the same number of columns with compatible data types per position
Result column names come from the first SELECT statement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the duplicate-removal difference
Correctly states the column-count/data-type compatibility requirement
Mentions the performance implication of the dedup pass

questions.title: Building a grouped Tablix with subtotals
questions.prompt: Describe how you'd configure a Tablix in SSRS Report Builder so that AdventureWorks2012 sales data is grouped by ProductCategory, with each category showing a subtotal of SalesAmount, plus a single grand total at the very bottom of the whole report.
questions.modelAnswer: Start with a Tablix bound to a dataset that includes ProductCategory and SalesAmount. In the Row Groups pane at the bottom of the designer, right-click the existing detail group and choose Add Group > Parent Group, grouping by ProductCategory -- this inserts a new group header/footer row pair around the detail rows and adds a ProductCategory textbox automatically. To get a subtotal per category, right-click the SalesAmount cell in the detail row and choose Add Total; SSRS inserts a =Sum(Fields!SalesAmount.Value) expression into the new group's footer row, and because that textbox lives inside the ProductCategory group's footer, Sum() automatically scopes itself to just that group's rows -- no explicit scope argument is needed. For the grand total, add a second total, but this time on the outermost table (body) row rather than inside any group -- the same Sum(Fields!SalesAmount.Value) expression, placed outside every group's scope, sums across the entire dataset instead of just one category's rows. The key mechanic throughout is that Sum() defaults to whatever scope (group, table, or dataset) the textbox containing it actually sits in, unless a second argument explicitly names a different scope.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this from the inside out: detail rows first, bound to SalesAmount, then right-click to add a parent group on ProductCategory, which gives me a header and footer row around each category's detail rows automatically. For the category subtotal, I right-click the SalesAmount cell and choose Add Total, which drops a Sum() expression right into that group's new footer -- and because of where that textbox physically sits, it already knows to only sum rows inside that one category's group, with no extra configuration from me. The grand total is the same idea one level up: I add a total on the outer table row, outside any group, and that Sum() expression now scopes to the entire table instead of one category. The thing I'd double check before calling it done is that I haven't accidentally copied a group-scoped Sum() expression into the grand-total row, because a textbox's scope comes from its physical location in the Tablix, not from the expression text itself.
questions.example:
-- Category subtotal (in the ProductCategory group footer row):
=Sum(Fields!SalesAmount.Value)

-- Grand total (in the outer table/body row, outside any group):
=Sum(Fields!SalesAmount.Value)
-- Same expression text -- the difference is entirely the row's scope.
commonMistakes: Placing the grand-total expression inside a group's footer by mistake, so it only sums that one group instead of the whole report
Assuming Sum() needs an explicit scope argument for a simple case like this, instead of relying on the textbox's own location
Forgetting Add Group > Parent Group is what actually inserts the new header/footer rows, rather than editing the detail row directly
Not verifying each category's subtotal against a manual SUM in SSMS before trusting the report
keyPoints: A parent group on ProductCategory adds a header/footer row pair around the detail rows
Add Total inserts a Sum() expression into the group's footer, scoped to that group automatically
A total placed outside any group (table/body scope) sums the entire dataset for the grand total
Sum()'s scope comes from the textbox's location in the Tablix, not from the expression itself

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes adding the ProductCategory group
Correctly describes the category subtotal mechanism and its automatic scope
Correctly describes the grand total's different scope

questions.title: SUM inflated after joining a one-to-many table
questions.prompt: A query joins SalesOrderHeader to SalesOrderDetail and correctly totals each order with SUM(LineTotal). After adding a third join to a Promotion table -- where some orders have more than one matching promotion row -- the total for those specific orders suddenly doubles or triples, even though nothing about the actual sales changed. The join conditions are all correct and genuinely relate the tables. What's going on, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a Cartesian product -- every join condition is correct and genuinely relates the tables -- it's join fan-out, which happens whenever a correct join still has a one-to-many relationship on one side. Each SalesOrderDetail row that matches more than one Promotion row gets physically duplicated once per matching promotion before SUM ever runs, so SUM(LineTotal) is now adding the same line total two or three times for any order whose promotion happens to match more than once, while orders with exactly one (or zero) matching promotions are unaffected. The fix is to never combine two separate one-to-many expansions in a single flat join and then aggregate at the end -- instead, pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the grain actually needed, in its own subquery or CTE, before joining. Here, that means computing the order total from SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail alone first, and only joining Promotion afterward (or in a separate query) if promotion details are genuinely needed, rather than letting its fan-out multiply rows that feed directly into the order-total SUM.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out first that this isn't the Cartesian-product bug people usually learn about -- every join condition here is correct and really does relate the tables. This is fan-out: joining in a table that can legitimately match more than one row per order duplicates the order-detail rows underneath it, once per matching promotion, before the SUM even runs. So an order with two matching promotions gets its LineTotal counted twice, not because the math is wrong, but because the row genuinely got duplicated first. My fix is to separate the two aggregations: compute each order's total from just SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail in a CTE first, completely isolated from the Promotion join, and only bring Promotion into a separate query (or join it after the order total is already locked in) if I actually need promotion-level detail. The rule I'd apply going forward is never to let two independent one-to-many joins sit in the same flat query feeding one aggregate -- pre-aggregate each one to the grain I need first.
questions.example:
-- WRONG: Promotion's fan-out inflates the order total
SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
JOIN Sales.SpecialOfferProduct promo ON promo.ProductID = sod.ProductID
GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID;

-- FIXED: order total computed in isolation, before any promotion join
WITH OrderTotals AS (
    SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
    FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
    JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
    GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID
)
SELECT * FROM OrderTotals;
commonMistakes: Assuming a correct, relating join condition rules out row duplication entirely
Not comparing row counts (or a known-good total) before and after adding the third join
Reaching for SUM(DISTINCT ...) as a quick fix, which only coincidentally works and breaks again as soon as two genuinely different line totals happen to match
Combining two separate one-to-many expansions in one flat query feeding a single aggregate, instead of pre-aggregating each one to the grain actually needed
keyPoints: A correct join condition can still fan out rows when the relationship is genuinely one-to-many
Fan-out duplicates rows before aggregation runs, inflating any SUM downstream
This is distinct from a Cartesian product, which comes from a missing or non-relating join condition
Fix: pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the needed grain in its own subquery/CTE before joining further

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses join fan-out (not a Cartesian product)
Explains why the duplication inflates the SUM
Proposes a correct fix (pre-aggregating before joining further)

questions.title: A Flat File Source that suddenly won't parse
questions.prompt: An SSIS package has loaded the same vendor CSV file successfully every night for months. Tonight it fails at the Flat File Source with an error like 'The column delimiter for column 4 was not found.' Nobody touched the package. What's the most likely cause, and how would you confirm and fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: A Flat File Connection Manager's column layout -- delimiters, column count, text qualifier -- is configured once, against a sample of the file, and saved as a fixed definition; it does not re-detect or adapt to the file's structure on later runs. This exact pattern -- worked for months, suddenly fails, package itself unchanged -- almost always means the upstream vendor changed the file's actual structure: a column was added or removed, a free-text field that never used to contain the delimiter character now does (common with an unqualified comma-delimited file and no text qualifier configured), or an extra header or footer row was introduced. The way to confirm it is to open the actual current file directly -- not just trust the connection manager's cached preview -- and compare its real column count and content against the Flat File Connection Manager's Columns page. The fix is to update the connection manager to match the file's new real structure: adjust the column count, add or correct the text qualifier if a field can legitimately contain the delimiter, or adjust how many header/footer rows are skipped, then re-validate with the Preview button before re-running the package.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move wouldn't be to open the SSIS package at all -- it'd be to open the actual file that landed tonight and just look at it. A Flat File Connection Manager's column definition is locked in whenever it was first configured; it has no way to notice on its own that the vendor's file changed shape. 'Worked for months, broke overnight, nothing in the package changed' is close to a textbook signature for exactly that -- an extra column got added, or a text field that used to be delimiter-safe now has a comma in it with no text qualifier set up to protect against that. Once I've actually compared tonight's file to what the connection manager expects, the fix is just updating the connection manager to match reality -- column count, text qualifier, header rows -- and then hitting Preview before I trust it enough to re-run the whole package.
commonMistakes: Assuming the package itself broke and debugging SSIS logic before ever opening the actual file
Trusting the connection manager's cached preview instead of looking at the file that actually landed tonight
Forgetting to configure a text qualifier for free-text fields that could legitimately contain the delimiter character
Changing the connection manager's settings without re-validating with Preview before re-running the package
keyPoints: A Flat File Connection Manager's column layout is fixed at configuration time and doesn't adapt automatically
This failure pattern (worked for months, package unchanged, sudden failure) usually means the source file's structure changed upstream
Confirm by comparing the actual current file against the connection manager's Columns page
Fix by updating the connection manager (column count, text qualifier, header rows) to match the file's real structure, then re-validate with Preview

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies an upstream file-structure change as the likely cause
Describes a practical way to confirm it (comparing the actual file to the connection manager)
Proposes the correct fix and re-validation step

questions.title: Why Dev, QA, and Production stay separate
questions.prompt: Why does a BI team typically maintain separate Dev, QA, and Production SQL Server environments, and promote a change through them in that fixed order, instead of just building and testing directly against the Production database that live reports and real users already depend on?
questions.modelAnswer: Dev is where new work is actually built, and it's expected to be unstable -- half-finished packages, broken queries, and throwaway test data are all normal there, and critically, none of that instability is visible to anyone who depends on real numbers. QA is a separate, more stable environment with data that resembles Production, used specifically to verify a change behaves correctly before any real user is ever exposed to it -- this is where testing is supposed to happen, not in Dev and not in Production. Production is the environment real business users and live reports actually run against, and it's deliberately the last environment any change reaches, only after being built in Dev and then validated in QA. Testing directly against Production is risky for two concrete reasons: an in-progress or buggy change can lock, corrupt, or simply show wrong numbers in data that live reports depend on right now, and there's no safe way to test something genuinely risky -- a schema change, a large bulk load -- without potentially causing a real outage if it goes wrong. Promoting a change through Dev, then QA, then Production in that fixed order guarantees every change gets at least one chance to fail somewhere that doesn't matter yet before it ever reaches somewhere that does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it around what's allowed to break where. Dev is allowed to break -- that's the whole point of it, it's where I'm actively building and nobody real is looking at it. QA is where I prove a change actually works against data that looks like the real thing, before any real user sees it. Production is the one environment where breaking something has an actual business cost, so it's deliberately the last stop, not the first. If I skipped straight to testing in Production, the two real risks are: a change that's still buggy could corrupt or lock data that a live report is reading from right now, and there's no safe way to rehearse something genuinely risky, like a schema change, without actually risking the outage I was trying to avoid. The fixed Dev-then-QA-then-Production order is really just making sure every change gets tested somewhere low-stakes before it reaches somewhere high-stakes.
commonMistakes: Making a direct change in Production 'just this once' to save time
Treating QA as optional for a change that 'seems small' instead of validating it there first
Letting QA's data drift so far from Production's that it stops catching real issues
Conflating Dev and QA as the same environment instead of recognizing their different purposes (building vs. validating)
keyPoints: Dev is for building and is expected to be unstable, isolated from real users
QA validates a change against production-like data before any real user is exposed to it
Production is the last environment reached, only after Dev and QA
Direct Production changes risk live data and can't safely rehearse risky operations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the purpose of each environment (Dev, QA, Production)
Correctly explains the risk of testing directly in Production
Explains why the promotion order matters

questions.title: Why the semantic model is its own layer
questions.prompt: In Power BI, what is a semantic model (also called a dataset), and why is it treated as a layer separate from any one report built on top of it? What becomes possible once you realize several different reports can all point at the very same semantic model?
questions.modelAnswer: A semantic model is the published data model itself -- tables, relationships, calculated columns, measures, and RLS roles -- without any particular report's visuals attached to it; it's the single source of truth layer sitting between raw data and however many reports choose to visualize it. Publishing a single .pbix that has both a model and report visuals does create a semantic model and a report together by default, but once published, the semantic model exists in the workspace as its own independent object. Any report author with the right permission can then build a brand-new report connected to that existing semantic model (through Create report, or a Live Connection) without rebuilding the tables, relationships, or measures from scratch. This matters because it means business logic -- how a measure is calculated, which relationships are correct, who can see which rows under RLS -- is defined exactly once, and every report built against that semantic model automatically inherits the same correct logic; if a measure's definition ever needs fixing, fixing it once in the semantic model updates every report built on top of it, instead of requiring the same fix to be found and repeated across several separately-built reports.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the semantic model as the thing that actually has the business logic in it -- the relationships, the measures, the RLS roles -- completely separate from however a given report chooses to visualize that logic. Publishing one .pbix does hand you both a semantic model and a report at the same time, but they're two separate objects the moment they land in the workspace, and that's exactly what lets a finance team build one report and an executive-summary team build a completely different-looking report, both connected live to that same underlying semantic model, without either of them re-deriving what 'Total Revenue' actually means. The real payoff is maintenance: if I find a bug in a measure, I fix it once, in the semantic model, and every report built on top of it -- including ones I didn't build myself -- picks up the fix automatically, instead of me having to track down and patch the same formula in five separate files.
commonMistakes: Rebuilding the same measures and relationships from scratch in every new report instead of connecting to the existing semantic model
Thinking a published semantic model and a published report are the same object
Not realizing RLS lives on the semantic model, so it applies consistently to every report connected to it
Forgetting a Live Connection report depends on that semantic model staying published and accessible
keyPoints: A semantic model is the data model (tables, relationships, measures, RLS) without any one report's visuals
Publishing a .pbix creates a semantic model and a report, but they become separate objects in the workspace
Multiple reports can connect to one shared semantic model via Live Connection
Fixing logic once in the semantic model updates every report built on top of it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a semantic model and what it contains
Correctly explains that it's a separate object from any one report
Explains the maintenance/consistency benefit of multiple reports sharing one model

questions.title: Asking for help when you're stuck
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time early in a project when you didn't know how to do something and had to ask a teammate or a more senior developer for help. How did you approach that conversation, and what did you do with the answer afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a behavioral question testing resourcefulness and whether a candidate can ask for help effectively, rather than either staying silently stuck or outsourcing the thinking entirely to someone else. A strong answer shows an attempt was made first -- checking documentation, trying an approach, forming a specific theory -- since teams value someone who tries before asking, but it should also show the candidate didn't stay stuck in silence for an unreasonably long time out of fear of looking unprepared. When actually asking, the question should be specific -- naming what was tried and exactly where it broke down -- rather than a vague 'it's not working,' since a specific question gets a faster and more useful answer. The Action should also cover what happened after getting the answer: not just copying the fix, but understanding why it worked, so the same category of problem doesn't require asking again. Result should state a concrete outcome using STAR -- being unblocked within some stated timeframe, and ideally applying the same concept independently on a later, similar problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell one specific story. Situation: early in my capstone, I couldn't get an OLE DB Destination's fast-load mode to actually speed anything up, and I'd already tried switching the data access mode and rereading the component's tooltips with no luck. Task: I needed to actually understand what I was missing, not just make the error go away. Action: I asked a more experienced developer a specific question -- 'I switched to fast load, but it's still inserting one row at a time based on the execution time, here's what I've already tried' -- rather than just saying it wasn't working. They pointed out I still had the destination's table lock option unchecked, which was serializing the insert behind other activity on the table. Result: once I checked that option, the load time dropped noticeably, and I started checking that same setting by default on every OLE DB Destination I've built since, without needing to ask again. I'd keep the story specific and make sure it lands on that last point -- what I actually learned to do differently afterward.
commonMistakes: Staying stuck in silence for too long before asking, out of fear of looking unprepared
Asking a vague question ('it's not working') instead of naming what was tried and exactly where it broke down
Copying the fix without understanding why it worked, so the same type of problem requires asking again later
Describing a general attitude toward asking for help instead of telling one specific, real story with a stated Result
keyPoints: Show an attempt was made before asking, but don't stay stuck in silence too long either
Ask a specific question naming what was tried and where it broke down
Understand why the answer worked rather than just copying it
Use STAR and state a concrete Result, including what changed afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows a reasonable attempt was made before asking for help
Tells a specific, real story using STAR
States a concrete Result, including what was learned or applied afterward
